section_summary: This section consists chiefly of petitions and letters from churches, civic groups, labor representatives, educators, veterans, parents, and private citizens demanding an end to American exports that supported Japan’s war in China. State Department replies repeatedly explained that the Neutrality Act could embargo only enumerated arms and only after a presidential finding of war, which would affect China as well as Japan, while scrap iron, oil, and similar commodities remained outside presidential control. The section also includes an antiwar publicity leaflet, organizational resolutions, congressional referrals, and later replies noting that licensing of aircraft and aeronautical supplies for countries bombing civilians had virtually ceased.

subfiles.title: Church Council of Sacramento resolution against shipments of war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: Church Council of Sacramento; John P. Woodard, president
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: The council asks the federal government to stop sales and shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Church Council of Sacramento resolution cites destruction of Chinese universities and mission schools and Nanking atrocities, arguing Japan depends on imported munitions materials and urging federal action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to John P. Woodard
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked to stop exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reply to John Woodard: a presidential war proclamation would embargo arms to Japan and China, other commodities are uncovered, with export-license totals and the government's condemnation of civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Joseph F. Griggs’s protest concerning aid to China and supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: Mrs. Joseph F. Griggs
subfiles.about: Griggs asks why Americans are urged to support Chinese relief while shipments sustaining Japan’s war cannot be stopped.
subfiles.summary: Although badly degraded in the OCR, the letter contrasts American relief for China with American supplies reaching Japan. Griggs asks Sayre to explain why shipments of war materials cannot be halted and appeals to American sympathy for China.

subfiles.title: Enclosed account concerning the war in China
subfiles.about: A fragmentary account discusses the effects of the war and appeals for American help rather than assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Garbled enclosure on the war in China, apparently urging America to aid Chinese victims and keep Chinese goodwill rather than encourage Japan's policy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. Joseph F. Griggs
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department answers Griggs’s protest by outlining the legal limits of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply says a finding of war would stop enumerated arms shipments to both China and Japan, while the Act did not authorize restrictions on other commodities. It reports licensed export values and repeats the government’s condemnation of civilian bombing and discouragement of aircraft exports that materially supported it.

subfiles.title: Louis Pollock letter advocating an embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Louis Pollock, Ohio Valley Labor News
subfiles.about: Pollock urges the President to invoke neutrality legislation and end financial and commercial relations supporting Japan.
subfiles.summary: Speaking for organized labor, Pollock argues that American munitions, oil, cotton, and other goods were indispensable to Japan’s war in China. He calls for an embargo and invokes Spain as a contrasting case in which the United States embargoed the recognized government while arming China’s enemy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Louis Pollock
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the Neutrality Act and the absence of legal authority to prohibit most exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply emphasizes that a war proclamation would embargo arms to both belligerents and that the statute did not reach commodities beyond listed arms and implements of war. It provides export-license totals for China and Japan and encloses the Neutrality Act and the pamphlet International Traffic in Arms.

subfiles.title: Charles K. Imbrie letter forwarding an antiwar circular
subfiles.from: Charles K. Imbrie
subfiles.about: Imbrie asks whether claims that the United States was materially supporting Japan’s war are true and whether the relationship can be ended.
subfiles.summary: Charles Imbrie forwards an antiwar circular whose charges, if true, are serious, and asks whether the U.S. can cease complicity in slaughter in the Far East.

subfiles.title: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression leaflet
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The leaflet urges Americans to campaign against the sale of military supplies and strategic materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The leaflet quotes Americans in China who associated Japanese attacks with American scrap iron, trucks, aircraft fuel, bombs, and chemicals. It argues that relief donations cannot offset American economic support for Japanese forces and asks readers to write national officials, distribute literature, organize local committees, and contribute funds. It also lists the committee’s sponsors and national board.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Charles K. Imbrie
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds to Imbrie’s concerns about American supplies used by Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reply to Imbrie: the Neutrality Act could halt listed arms only after a war proclamation, applying equally to China; scrap iron and oil are uncovered, with license totals and opposition to civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: Mildred H. McAfee letter protesting exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Mildred H. McAfee
subfiles.about: McAfee asks the President and Congress to end the traffic in American materials used in Japan’s war against China.
subfiles.summary: Mildred McAfee lists American materials, aircraft and oil allegedly sustaining Japan's war, arguing the trade makes the U.S. a partner in destroying the Chinese people.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mildred H. McAfee
subfiles.from: B. Walton Moore, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges McAfee’s views and sets out the administration’s legal position on exports.
subfiles.summary: The response welcomes informed public opinion but says the Neutrality Act would embargo listed arms to both China and Japan if invoked. It gives licensed-export totals and notes that the government had condemned civilian bombing and communicated that position to aircraft and aeronautical-equipment exporters.

subfiles.title: Board of Foreign Missions letter transmitting a resolution
subfiles.from: R. E. Diffendorfer and W. E. Shaw, corresponding secretaries
subfiles.about: The secretaries forward a resolution adopted by the Methodist Episcopal Board of Foreign Missions concerning China.
subfiles.summary: Methodist Episcopal Board of Foreign Missions, with over four million members and 551 missionaries, transmits a resolution and requests continued government action.

subfiles.title: Methodist Episcopal Board of Foreign Missions resolution
subfiles.from: Board of Foreign Missions of the Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.about: The board condemns Japanese atrocities in China and petitions for an end to American exports supporting the invasion.
subfiles.summary: Methodist board resolution denouncing looting, indiscriminate bombing and slaughter in Japan's invasion, saying American commerce must yield to humanitarian interests.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to the Board of Foreign Missions
subfiles.from: B. Walton Moore, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Board of Foreign Missions of the Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the board’s resolution and explains existing export law.
subfiles.summary: The reply thanks the board for sending the resolution to the President and Secretary of State. It says the Neutrality Act could embargo listed arms only to both belligerents following a proclamation, provides license totals, and reiterates opposition to civilian bombing and its encouragement through aircraft exports.

subfiles.title: Eugene Women’s City Club petition and signatures
subfiles.from: Members of the Women’s City Club of Eugene
subfiles.about: Members ask Hull to use his influence to halt exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The brief handwritten petition requests action against shipments aiding Japan. Its second page contains the names and addresses of numerous Eugene-area members who endorsed the appeal.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to an Eugene Women’s City Club member
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds to the Eugene club petition by explaining the legal limits of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that invoking the Act would halt listed arms exports to China as well as Japan and that no authority existed to stop other commodities. It supplies license totals and encloses the congressional resolution and an explanatory pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Herbert F. Loomis letter opposing military supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: Herbert F. Loomis
subfiles.about: Loomis asks the administration to end American participation in Japan’s destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: Herbert Loomis calls military supplies to Japan complicity in slaughter and folly, strengthening a potential aggressor while building American forces.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Herbert F. Loomis
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department answers Loomis by summarizing the Neutrality Act and licensed arms exports.
subfiles.summary: The response says that a presidential finding of war would bar enumerated arms to both China and Japan, while other commodities remained beyond the Act. It reports export-license totals and includes copies of the relevant resolution and pamphlet.

subfiles.title: L. Theron French letter conveying a church conference resolution
subfiles.from: L. Theron French
subfiles.about: French reports a unanimous church request that the President curtail shipments of arms and war-making materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Methodist Tabernacle conference recognizes statutory limits but asks Roosevelt to do everything possible, condemning profiteers and shame that American materials enabled Japan's invasion.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to L. Theron French
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the church’s request and explains why the Neutrality Act had not stopped exports.
subfiles.summary: The reply thanks French for conveying the conference’s views and says a war proclamation would embargo arms to China as well as Japan. It distinguishes covered arms from other commodities, gives export-license totals, and encloses the statute and explanatory pamphlet.

subfiles.title: George P. Millar Camp resolution against scrap-iron shipments
subfiles.from: Lawrence Perry and George P. Millar Camp No. 31, United Spanish War Veterans
subfiles.about: The veterans’ camp petitions the government to stop all shipments of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Camp resolution asks the government to stop scrap-iron and other war-material exports out of concern for women and children and a desire for strict neutrality.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Lawrence Perry
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that scrap iron was outside the statutory list of arms subject to embargo.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges the veterans’ resolution and explains that a Neutrality Act proclamation would apply to both China and Japan. It specifically notes that scrap iron was not enumerated as an arm or implement of war and that no existing statute authorized the President to prohibit its export.

subfiles.title: Mrs. B. B. Boyle letter urging enforcement or amendment of neutrality policy
subfiles.from: Mrs. B. B. Boyle
subfiles.about: Boyle protests America’s material contribution to Japan’s war and asks Hull to use his influence to stop it.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Boyle praises Hull's peace efforts but says America is not staying out of the war while Japan gets much of its supply from the U.S., condemning profits.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. B. B. Boyle
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department answers Boyle’s protest with its standard explanation of neutrality law and export policy.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that a finding of war would impose an arms embargo on both sides and that non-arms commodities could not be prohibited under the Act. It gives license totals and repeats the government’s condemnation of civilian bombing and its representations to airplane and aeronautical-equipment exporters.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s routing memorandum to Dr. Hornbeck
subfiles.from: Office of the Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Under Secretary’s office requests preparation of a reply.
subfiles.summary: This brief internal routing slip sends the associated matter to Dr. Hornbeck. Its sole instruction is to prepare a response.

subfiles.title: Akron Ministerial Association letter on Japan and neutrality legislation
subfiles.from: George P. Snyder, Akron Ministerial Association
subfiles.about: The association condemns Japan’s aggression and proposes amending the Neutrality Act to permit discrimination against an aggressor.
subfiles.summary: Akron ministers charge Japan with violating the Kellogg-Briand Pact and propose letting the President, with Congress, designate an aggressor and use American power against it.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles reply to George P. Snyder
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles acknowledges the Akron Ministerial Association’s views on the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Welles thanks Snyder's association for its convictions, saying the government is intensively considering the issues for American and humanitarian interests.

subfiles.title: Dow W. Harter letter forwarding Snyder’s proposal
subfiles.from: Dow W. Harter
subfiles.about: Harter asks for the State Department’s views on the Akron ministers’ proposal to amend the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Dow Harter forwards George Snyder's proposal for presidential designation of an aggressor with congressional approval and requests guidance.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles reply to Dow W. Harter
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles tells Harter that Congress will likely consider amendments to the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Welles notes that he received an identical letter directly from Snyder and encloses his acknowledgment. He says Congress would probably review the need for amendments in light of international developments and proposals from multiple sources, then returns Snyder’s letter.

subfiles.title: D. Lane Powers letter forwarding a constituent petition
subfiles.from: D. Lane Powers
subfiles.about: Powers forwards a petition from constituents concerning the sale of raw war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Congressman Powers transmits a petition from residents of his New Jersey district for the Secretary's information.

subfiles.title: New Jersey residents’ petition against trade supporting Japan
subfiles.from: Mabel D. Macintosh and other petitioners
subfiles.to: Government of the United States, via D. Lane Powers
subfiles.about: The petition asks the government to end American trade that supported Japan’s destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition cites Japan’s alleged violations of the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact and condemns bombings of undefended cities. It lists American raw materials, planes, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks used by Japan and invokes the Good Neighbor principle in demanding every practicable means to end the traffic.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to D. Lane Powers
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hull supplies material Powers can use to answer petitioners and describes a tightening of aircraft-export licensing.
subfiles.summary: Hull's reply to Powers: a proclamation would embargo arms to both sides, other commodities are uncovered, and aircraft licenses to countries bombing civilians have virtually ceased.

subfiles.title: Arthur B. Jenks letter forwarding a Parent-Teachers Association protest
subfiles.from: Arthur B. Jenks
subfiles.about: Jenks forwards the Whipple School Parent-Teachers Association’s protest and asks for comment.
subfiles.summary: Congressman Jenks forwards a Parent-Teachers Association protest against Japan's aggression and American sales of war supplies, requesting the Secretary's observations.

subfiles.title: Whipple School Parent-Teachers Association letter to Arthur Jenks
subfiles.from: Julia F. Butler and Leroy C. Moore, Whipple School Parent-Teachers Association
subfiles.about: The association urges Jenks to support legislation ending American war-supply sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Whipple School PTA condemns Japan's aggression and American profiteers supplying over half its munitions, and demands legislation even at risk of offending Japan.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to Arthur B. Jenks
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hull provides a suggested explanation of the Neutrality Act for the Whipple School association.
subfiles.summary: The reply says invoking the Act would stop enumerated arms shipments to China as well as Japan and that no authority existed to prohibit other commodities. It supplies export-license totals, encloses the statute and International Traffic in Arms, and returns the association’s letter.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. W. W. Banner
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Banner’s papers about conditions in China and returns her enclosures.
subfiles.summary: The letter refers to a copy of correspondence from missionary Virginia M. Atkinson and explains the Neutrality Act’s limited application to listed arms after a presidential proclamation. It supplies export-license totals, repeats the government’s condemnation of civilian bombing, and returns Banner’s original enclosures and stamped envelope.

subfiles.title: Office of Arms and Munitions Control memorandum concerning Virginia M. Atkinson
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Yost asks Far Eastern Affairs whether the reply to Banner should address the reported imprisonment and property loss of missionary Virginia M. Atkinson.
subfiles.summary: Arms and Munitions Control memo: Atkinson was a Shanghai prisoner with her China home wrecked; Yost suggests Far Eastern Affairs supply paragraphs for the reply.
